issues.title: Transaction tokens are not Access Tokens
issues.author: PieterKas
issues.body:
I would propose that instead of issuing a transaction token in response to the challenge, the authorisation server should issue an access token with some kind of indicator that the user has approved the explicit transaction and maybe with some additional claims, maybe as RAR claims, and then have that presented back to the resource server.

Transaction tokens are really designed to carry transaction context based on the access token and are requested by the resource server, not by the client. Having the client pass around transaction tokens and then using a transaction token effectively as an access token feels problematic. I think just re-casting this as an access token with some specific claims that indicate that the user did approve the specific transaction is more likely to provide a smooth integration path that's going to be safer and easier to integrate rather than this sort of unusual flow of a transaction token being issued to a client, which is then presented to a resource server, which treats it as an access token.

issues.title: Could this be built on CIBA?
issues.author: PieterKas
issues.body:
Thinking about this flow compared to CIBA, the main observation is that this flow adds the resource server interaction into the flow that is absent from CIBA, but once you get to the client/AS interactions, it shares many features with CIBA. What if the only part that needs to be added is the interaction with the RS, which signals specific details that needs to be used, and then passing that as the login_hint token.

It also requries switching the thing that gets provisioned to the client back to a OAuth access token, which I think is better than having transaction tokens as access tokens (we actually just added a section to the trasnaction token spec to make it explicit that it should not be used that way https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-transaction-tokens/pull/345)

issues.title: 4.4 Agent Relay: no mention of processing in intermediate relaying agent
issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body:
While the processing is client for the Client as defined in section 4.5, it would be important to mention that any intermediate agent relaying the `transaction_challenge` must do the same or at least must ensure that the Challenge is still a viable one to propagate.

I recommend the following text:

> In deployments where one agent delegates work to another agent, a transaction authorization challenge MAY be relayed through one or more intermediate agents before reaching the client. Each agent that relays the challenge MUST validate the challenge signature, issuer, and expiration then MUST relay it without modification if valid. An intermediate agent MUST NOT replace the challenge with a new challenge unless it is itself acting as a protected resource for a distinct operation and generates a new signed transaction authorization challenge for that operation.

issues.title: Why is the Transaction Authorization request not a new Grant Flow type?
issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body:
Having the Transaction Authorization request as a Grant has multiple advantages as it will be automatically support all the extension of OAuth and could be supported on existing Authorize and Token endpoints that decides to extend to this.

This would align the proposal to the usual issuance model of OAuth, Device Code Grant Flow,  and CIBA from which it is inspired from.

This will simplify the proposal by removing the need for transaction_authorization_endpoint in AS metadata as the token endpoint already exists.

issues.title: Obtaining undelegated access.
issues.author: PieterKas
issues.body:
The spec says:

The party that initiated an operation is not always the party authorized to approve it. For example,
an agent acting on behalf of one user might request access to a resource owned or controlled by
another user. The protected resource can determine that approval from the resource owner, or
from another party authorized to act for that resource owner, is required before the operation
can proceed.

Should an agent be able to obtain an access token on-behalf of a user that has not explictly delegated to it already?

comments.author: njwatson32
comments.body: At the very least the draft shouldn't _assume_ that ATs are JWTs, which it seems to do in §4.6: `the access token issued in response to the challenge will use the protected resource identified by the iss claim as its audience`.

issues.title: Can we remove the token-response authorization_details parameter?
issues.author: PieterKas
issues.body:
PR #10 returns granted authorization_details both inside the access token (the copy the protected resource validates) and as the token-response parameter required by RFC 9396 §7.

The response parameter is a MUST in RFC 9396. In this draft the client typically acts as a relay and may not need the granted details, and surfacing them in plaintext to the client (and any relaying agent) has data-minimisation implications for sensitive operations (e.g. payment amount, creditor, account).

1. Does the client in this flow have a genuine need for the response-parameter copy, or is the in-token copy sufficient?
2. Can/should this draft deviate from RFC 9396 to make it optional?

issues.title: Access Token not sufficient as unique output of a Transaction Challenge
issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body:
The Draft is about implementing a Challenge / Response for the confirmation for dedicated set of transaction details.

While effectively RAR is focused on supporting the issuance of least privileges and more constrained Access Tokens, the scenario seems more importantly to point at supporting [Transactions Tokens ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens/) as a first class output,

I recommend the authors to extend the support to both class of tokens.

issues.title: Transaction Authorization Challenge must support option of DPoP key binding for issued Access Token
issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body: If the outcome of the flow is an Access Toke, there must be an option to allow the token to be bound to a Resource Server owned key as the Access Token is of type `Bearer`.

issues.title: Twice is mentionned that the Access Token must not be modified, but can it be?
issues.author: identitymonk
issues.body:
I feel there is extra cautiousness on the aspect of multi agent interaction. Twice the Authors mentioned in section 6.1 that:

-  Each agent that relays the access token MUST relay it without modification. 
- The agent MUST NOT modify the access token.

But can the Access Token be modified? It is a JWT that follows the BCP therefore protected by Signature, therefore if an Agent would modify it, the whole exchange would crumble anyway as a fail safe mechanism.

Therefore, those should be dropped and replace by a statement that presentation of the Access Token should follow the latest BCP.

issues.title: Use OAuth Deferred Token Response for the asynchronous authorization flow
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem
The draft defines its own asynchronous mechanism for obtaining transaction authorization: a dedicated transaction authorization endpoint, a `transaction_authorization_id`, and a device-grant-style polling loop (`authorization_pending`/`slow_down`, based on RFC 8628). This re-implements, in this spec, a general capability — defer a token decision and poll for it — that is being standardized separately.

## Proposal
Reuse the OAuth Deferred Token Response (DTR) mechanism [`draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response`] as the async substrate:
- The client presents the transaction authorization challenge at the **token endpoint** via a new grant type `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:txn-authz-challenge`, signaling `completion_mode=deferred`.
- If approval is asynchronous, the AS returns a DTR deferred response (`400 authorization_pending` + `deferral_code`); the client polls via `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:deferred`.
- On approval, the token endpoint returns the access token — unchanged from today.

## Benefits
- Stops defining a bespoke endpoint and polling protocol; removes the RFC 8628 dependency.
- Inherits DTR's deferral-code sender-constraint, cancellation (revocation), and optional completion callbacks.
- Aligns the asynchronous pattern with the rest of OAuth at the token endpoint.

## Trade-offs / questions
- This introduces a **normative dependency** on [`draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response`], an early individual I-D. Is the WG comfortable depending on it now, or would an *informative* reference — retaining the current self-contained flow as a fallback until DTR matures — be preferable?
- Token endpoint + new grant type, vs. keeping a dedicated endpoint?

A PR implementing this is at #21 (independent, based on `main`).

issues.title: Key-binding option for the issued access token via assurance profiles
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
Follow-up to #18 (option to key-bind the issued access token, since it is otherwise a Bearer token). This proposes a concrete design and a PR implementing it.

## Proposal
- Add a `cnf` claim to the challenge naming the key the protected resource observed on the triggering request; the authorization server **sender-constrains** the issued access token to that key, and the protected resource verifies proof of possession on presentation. **DPoP** mandatory-to-implement, **mutual-TLS** optional.
- Express the *option* from #18 as two **assurance profiles**, selected per operation by the protected resource: **key-bound** (challenge carries `cnf` -> sender-constrained token) and **relay** (no `cnf` -> today's Bearer behavior).
- Because a key-bound token cannot be relayed to and presented by a different agent, add **delegation** across agents via OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (per-hop re-binding with an `act` chain).

## Benefits
- Closes the Bearer-replay/theft gap on the agent->RS leg (the leg the client can't otherwise authenticate on); gives verifiable requester context; works for public clients; preserves Bearer behavior as the relay profile.

## Question on #18's wording
#18 mentions binding to a *"Resource Server owned key."* This proposal binds the token to the **requesting agent's key** via DPoP/mTLS, which is the standard sender-constraint that makes the token non-Bearer and verifiable at the RS. If an RS-owned-key model (e.g., audience-restriction to an RS key) was intended instead, let's discuss — the mechanics differ.

issues.title: Externalized authorization (PEP/PDP, AuthZEN AARP): access token as a decision input, and carrying obligations
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem
In an externalized-authorization deployment, the protected resource is a **Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)** and the decision is made by a **Policy Decision Point (PDP)** (e.g. via the AuthZEN Authorization API). When the PDP cannot authorize an action *yet* because a prerequisite must first be met, the **AuthZEN Access Request and Approval Profile (AARP)** returns "not yet — here is the prerequisite," and re-evaluates once it is satisfied.

A transaction authorization challenge is a natural way to *satisfy* an AARP human-approval prerequisite. But the draft currently assumes the issued access token is the **final authorization the protected resource acts on** — which is exactly wrong for this deployment, where the enforcement point does not decide.

## Worked example
1. An agent tries to initiate a **£5,000 payment to "Example Ltd"** on the user's behalf.
2. The PEP asks the PDP to evaluate *(subject = agent, action = initiate, resource = payment £5000 → Example Ltd)*. Per AARP, the PDP responds **"pending — prerequisite: account-owner approval of this transaction."**
3. The PEP surfaces this as a **transaction authorization challenge**; the flow obtains the owner's approval and issues an access token that is *evidence the approval prerequisite was satisfied* (bound to `txn`, narrowed to that payment).
4. The PEP **re-submits the evaluation to the PDP, now presenting that access token as an input** (the satisfied prerequisite). The PDP re-evaluates and returns **permit — with obligations**, e.g. `write transaction-audit-log`, `notify account owner`, `single-use for this txn`.
5. The PEP **enforces those obligations** as it executes the payment.

## The two gaps this exposes
- **Token-as-verdict vs. token-as-input (steps 3→4).** The draft frames the access token as the authorization the protected resource acts on. Here the enforcement point does not decide — it feeds the token *back into the PDP* as one input to a subsequent decision. Nothing in the draft sanctions "this token is evidence a prerequisite was satisfied, which a PEP MAY feed into a downstream policy decision rather than treat as the verdict," so deployments must bend the language.
- **No carrier for obligations (steps 4→5).** The PDP's permit carries obligations the enforcement point must apply (`audit-log`, `notify`, `single-use`). The draft has no defined place to convey them, so there is no interoperable way to get them to the enforcer.

## Proposed direction (optional, additive, profile-agnostic)
- Allow the access token to be treated as **terminal** authorization *or* as **one input to a downstream policy decision** (e.g. a PDP); the draft's validation requirements apply either way.
- Allow **obligations** to be conveyed within the granted `authorization_details` or a claim defined by an application profile.

This keeps the core mechanism free of any dependency on AuthZEN while making it **bindable** by AuthZEN AARP / PEP-PDP deployments.

issues.title: Executing an approved transaction with a different key
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
With key-bound challenges (#29), the access token is bound to the key of agent A, which triggered the challenge. A party B with a different key cannot present it:
- another instance of A, such as a replica, or a replacement for one that lost its key while approval was pending;
- a sub-agent of A;
- another agent.

Today B triggers its own challenge, which may need a second approval: the approving party is interrupted again, may no longer be available, and the operation is delayed. That is the safe default, because each approval shows who will execute. Can B execute the approved transaction without another approval when policy allows?

The first decision is scope: should this draft address this, or leave it out of scope, keeping the second approval as the intended model and leaving re-binding to a separate specification?

**Proposal:** out of scope for this draft. Keep the second challenge as the intended model, and clarify that a protected resource may issue a new challenge with the same `txn` for the same operation, so an authorization server can reuse the approval under local policy. Leave re-binding by token exchange or delegation to a separate specification.

### Constraints
- **Authorization, not possession.** Holding A's challenge or token and proving B's key MUST NOT be enough. Re-binding needs evidence: B authenticates as A, A delegates to B, or a grant authorizes B. RFC 8693 leaves this to profiles (§1).
- **Same approval.** The same `txn`, audience and subject; equal or narrower `authorization_details`; no longer lifetime; single use across A and B. The requester context is unchanged or only adds B as the current actor (prior actors in `act` are informational, RFC 8693 §4.1).
- **Validation.** The protected resource needs a rule for accepting B's key instead of the challenge's `cnf`.

### Options
- **New challenge reusing the approval:** B gets its own challenge with the same `txn`, and the authorization server issues a token from the existing approval without asking again. The protected resource still vouches for B's key. Open: how B's request is linked to the `txn`, and who allows the reuse.
- **Token exchange (RFC 8693):** A's token is exchanged, with evidence, for one bound to B's key. Needs a profile for the evidence, who exchanges (B may not be a client of the authorization server), and validation.
- **Delegates named in the challenge:** rarely known when the challenge is issued, and needs a new claim.
- **No re-binding:** a second approval, documented as intended.

### Open questions
- Who vouches for B's key: the protected resource, A, or B at the authorization server?
- Is another instance of A a new actor, or only a new key?
- Delegation or transfer: can A still execute once B has a token?
- Must the approving party know about a change of executor?

Not part of this issue: propagating transaction context within the protected resource's trust domain, as in #23.

pulls.title: Issue #2: replace transaction token with access token + RAR authorization_details
pulls.author: PieterKas
pulls.body:
Addresses #2.

## Summary

This PR reframes the result of a transaction authorization challenge as an OAuth 2.1 access token whose granted `authorization_details` (per RFC 9396) describe the approved operation and bind the access token to the challenged transaction, instead of a transaction token issued under `draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens`.

Issue #2 argues that transaction tokens are designed to carry transaction context derived from an access token and are requested by the resource server, not the client. Using a transaction token as a bearer artifact carried by the client to the protected resource is an unusual pattern. Reusing the OAuth 2.1 access token abstraction:

- avoids defining a new bearer artifact carried by the client to the protected resource,
- lets existing access-token validation and protection mechanisms apply unchanged (including sender-constrained access tokens via DPoP / mTLS),
- aligns the response semantics with the standard OAuth 2.1 token endpoint response and the `authorization_details` response parameter defined in RFC 9396 §7,
- keeps the rest of the challenge mechanism intact: the challenge format, the asynchronous polling flow, the agent-relay rules, and the protected-resource metadata for challenge signing keys are unchanged.

The challenge still conveys the requested `authorization_details`; the authorization server still validates the challenge, obtains approval, and binds the result to the `txn` value. Only the issued artifact changes — from a `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:txn_token` carried in a `Txn-Token` header to a regular access token carried in the `Authorization` header.

## Changes

- **Abstract / Introduction** — describe the result as an access token whose granted authorization details describe the approved operation; drop the `draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens` dependency.
- **Conventions and Definitions** — remove the "transaction token" term; pull `authorization_details` into the definitions list referencing RFC 9396.
- **Architecture and Flow** — replace transaction-token wording (including the flow diagram label).
- **Challenge claims** — clarify that the access token issued in response carries granted `authorization_details` derived from the challenge.
- **Token response (`successful-access-token-response`)** — use the standard OAuth token-endpoint response format with the `authorization_details` response parameter; new example with `token_type: Bearer`, `expires_in`, and a granted `authorization_details` array.
- **New "Access Token" section** replacing "Transaction Token":
  - binding to the `txn` value from the challenge
  - granted `authorization_details` carried in the token (e.g. as JWT claim per RFC 9068 + RFC 9396 §9)
  - explicit scoping to the challenged operation — not a general-purpose access token
  - short lifetime; sender-constrained access tokens recommended for high-impact operations
- **Token presentation** — use the `Authorization` request header (Bearer / DPoP / mTLS) instead of the `Txn-Token` header.
- **Protected resource validation** — validate the access token, its `txn` binding, and that its granted `authorization_details` authorize the requested operation; explicit prohibition on honouring the granted authorization details for any operation other than the challenged one.
- **Security Considerations** — re-cast around access tokens; new paragraph requiring protected resources to evaluate granted `authorization_details` against the operation being requested so a token issued for one operation cannot authorize a different operation; carries forward replay, single-use, requester-context, and privacy guidance.
- **IANA** — no removals required; none of the previously registered items were transaction-token-specific.

## Open design points worth WG discussion

- Whether the access token issued in response to a challenge should be presentable alongside the original access token (two `Authorization`-equivalent credentials) or should replace it for the challenged request. The current text assumes a single Authorization header carrying the new access token; this matches RAR conventions but should be explicit if WG prefers otherwise.
- Whether `txn` should be REQUIRED in the access token (as drafted) or RECOMMENDED, given that the granted `authorization_details` alone may already pin the token to a specific operation in some deployments.
- Whether to mandate sender-constraint for the access token (currently SHOULD for high-impact, MAY otherwise).

## Test plan
- [ ] kramdown-rfc build succeeds (CI)
- [ ] HTML/text rendering review of new "Access Token" section and revised flow
- [ ] WG / shepherd review of the design points above

pulls.title: Use Deferred Token Response as the asynchronous substrate
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Implements the proposal in #20.

Replaces the bespoke transaction authorization endpoint and polling protocol with OAuth Deferred Token Response ([`draft-ietf-oauth-deferred-token-response`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-deferred-token-response/)):
- Present the challenge at the token endpoint via `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:txn-authz-challenge` with `completion_mode=deferred`.
- Defer with `400 authorization_pending` + `deferral_code`; poll via the deferred grant.
- A client that did not opt in to deferral and cannot be approved synchronously receives `access_denied`; it can retry with `completion_mode=deferred`.
- Remove the `transaction_authorization_endpoint` and `transaction_authorization_id` registrations; register the new grant type; discovery via `grant_types_supported` + `deferred_token_response_supported`.
- Replace `authorization_uri` with DTR's `interaction_required` state and `interaction_uri` parameter for approvals that need interaction.
- The access token response is unchanged.

**Notes**
- Tracks the DTR editor's copy at `oauth-wg/oauth-deferred-token-response@4001584` (ahead of -01): `interaction_required`/`interaction_uri`, base64url `deferral_code` examples, and the Substrate Invariants. The normative reference resolves to -00 until -01 is posted.
- **Open issue: access-token binding.** DTR's Sender-Constraint Requirements require a public client to send DPoP on the initial token request, and bind the access token issued on polling to that same client key; Substrate Guarantee 3 repeats this for every originating grant. In this draft the agent, not the client, presents the access token, so a token bound to the client's key is unusable by the agent. The draft states this and carries an Editor's Note; resolving it needs DTR to let the originating grant define access-token binding separately from deferral-code binding. Relates to #23.
- Based on `main`; builds cleanly with `kramdown-rfc`.
- **Normative dependency:** DTR is still an Internet-Draft, so the normative reference holds publication of this document until DTR is published; see #20 for the normative-vs-informative discussion.

pulls.title: Add key binding, assurance profiles, and delegation
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Addresses #18 (and proposed in #22).

Strengthens the sender-constrained access token the draft already recommends into a binding the protected resource can require and verify:
- Adds an **Agent Key and Proof of Possession** section (DPoP mandatory-to-implement, mutual-TLS optional) and a `cnf` claim in the challenge.
- Adds **Assurance Profiles**: key-bound (default; `cnf` present -> sender-constrained) and relay (no `cnf` -> current Bearer behavior) — this is the *option* requested in #18.
- In the key-bound profile the AS sender-constrains the access token and the PR verifies proof of possession.
- Adds **delegation across agents** via OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (a key-bound token can't be relayed to a different agent) and trust-domain propagation.

**Notes**
- Based on `main`, builds cleanly with `kramdown-rfc`, keeps the agent/Agent-Relay model, and is independent of my other proposals.
- See #18 for the "Resource Server owned key" wording question — this binds to the requesting agent's key (DPoP/mTLS).

pulls.title: Add access token key binding
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
Resolves #18. Supersedes #23.

### What
Lets a challenge carry a `cnf` claim identifying a binding key: a key proved on the triggering request. The authorization server binds the issued access token to that key using DPoP (RFC 9449) or mutual-TLS (RFC 8705).

Because the key is signed into the challenge, relays cannot change it, and a stolen challenge yields a token the thief cannot present. The client that submits the challenge need not hold the key, so this works for agents and for clients that call the protected resource directly.

### Why
Today the issued access token defaults to a bearer token, and it passes through the client and any intermediate agents. DPoP and mutual-TLS alone bind it to a key that the client proves, but the client is often not the party that presents the token. The protected resource already sees the presenter's key, so it carries that key in the challenge. Everything else is delegated to RFC 9449 and RFC 8705.

### Changes
- **Access Token Key Binding** (new section):
  - **Using an Existing Token Binding:** `cnf` is the key of the sender-constrained access token in the triggering request. No new client behavior.
  - **Establishing a Binding Key:** with a bearer token, `cnf` is the key of a DPoP proof sent with it, an explicit extension of RFC 9449, or of the mutual-TLS client certificate. Written as processing steps for the protected resource, including errors and the requester-context restriction.
- **`binding_key_required` error**, with `algs` as a `Bearer` parameter: asks for the request to be repeated with the same access token and a DPoP proof. Sent only to requests with `Accept-Txn-Challenge: ?1`. Registered in the OAuth Extensions Error registry.
- **Authorization server:** binds the token to the `cnf` key per RFC 9449 or RFC 8705, and to no other key. It does not verify possession; it relies on the protected resource's signed challenge. Client authentication still applies, with a scoped exception to `dpop_bound_access_tokens`. It accepts each challenge once and issues no refresh token.
- **Protected resource:** checks that the token is bound to the challenge's `cnf`.
- **Token response:** client-bound tokens go from RECOMMENDED to MAY, because an agent that is not the client cannot present them. The client relays the token and its `token_type` without holding the key.
- Security considerations, DPoP examples, and Bearer, DPoP and mutual-TLS as normative references.

### Review updates
be351c2 and e93235b address PieterKas's review: "binding key" terminology, the RFC 9449 extension made explicit with token-less proofs dropped, an explicit `binding_key_required` signal, and the authorization server trust model.

### Why this replaces #23
- **No new concepts.** #23's "Agent Key" and assurance profiles become the presence of `cnf`, which also works for ordinary clients.
- **Delegates.** RFC 9449 and RFC 8705 do the work. At issuance this PR adds only three rules: the key comes from the challenge, the client need not prove it, and no other key is used.
- **Removes a contradiction.** #23 re-bound tokens to a downstream agent's key through token exchange, but its own validation rejected them. Re-binding is dropped, and the delegation scenario is deferred to #30.
- **Specifies what #23 left open:**
  - DPoP proofs sent with bearer tokens, and how to request one;
  - the challenge's authentication scheme;
  - errors;
  - refresh tokens.
- **Drops:**
  - #23's mandatory-to-implement DPoP. The protected resource must instead know which methods the authorization server supports.
  - #23's trust-domain propagation section, which is unrelated to key binding.

### Left open
- **Execution with a different key**, such as by another agent instance or a sub-agent. That party obtains its own challenge for now. Deferred to #30.
- **Discovery of authorization server support** for binding keys. Configuration for now.
- **mTLS-only protected resources** have no specific signal for requesting a certificate-bound token.

### Also included, not specific to key binding
These close gaps in the base draft. I can split them out if you prefer.
- A challenge that fails validation gets `invalid_grant`, or a more specific RFC 6749 §5.2 code such as `unauthorized_client`.
- Single use is enforced per `txn` value, so two access tokens for one transaction cannot each be accepted.

### Validation
Builds cleanly with kramdown-rfc and xml2rfc. RFC section references are checked against the RFC text.

Thanks, all addressed:
- **Terminology and readability:** your suggestions are in; b1e6918 fixes the heading anchor and 8ced230 the `cnf` wording.
- **RFC 9449 alignment:** be351c2 states that this extends RFC 9449, requires `ath`, and drops token-less proofs.
- **Signalling:** be351c2 adds a self-contained `Bearer error="binding_key_required", algs="ES256"` response, with an example, for retrying with the same token and a DPoP proof; a `DPoP` challenge is sent only when a DPoP-bound token is required.
- **Trust model:** e93235b states that the authorization server does not verify possession and relies on the signed challenge, keeps client authentication, and makes a scoped exception to `dpop_bound_access_tokens`.

I think the intent here is that iinstead of doing POP at the AS, the client/agent can send a DPoP proof to the RS, which can confirm POP, and then put the cnf claim for which it wants a bindding into the challenge.

My other take is that this is an attempt to let the RS ask for a bound token, even if it previously accepted a bearer token (hence allowing a resource server to 'step-up" to a bound token for a specific trasnaction.

```suggestion
A binding key protects the access token issued for a challenge. The `cnf` claim is part of the signed challenge, so a party that relays the challenge cannot remove or replace the binding key. A party that does not hold the binding key, such as an intermediate agent, cannot present the access token. If that party submits the challenge itself, the resulting access token is bound to the same key, so it cannot present that token either. The authorization server accepts a challenge only once, so such a party can at most prevent the transaction from completing.
```

```suggestion
The strength of this protection depends on where the binding key comes from. If it is the key of a sender-constrained access token, a party that captured that token cannot substitute its own key. If it comes from a DPoP proof or a client certificate, it only shows that the sender of the triggering request holds the key. A party that obtained a bearer access token can then obtain a challenge with its own key as the binding key. Any requester context derived from that access token, such as an `act` claim ({{Section 4.1 of OAUTH-TOKEN-EXCHANGE}}), still identifies the original requester to the approving party. For this reason, {{access-token-key-binding}} restricts this source of binding keys when the protected resource relies on requester context.
```

```suggestion
This document extends the use of DPoP proofs defined in {{DPOP}}. A protected resource that supports binding keys can accept a DPoP proof on a request whose access token is not DPoP-bound, solely to determine the binding key. Such a proof does not authenticate the request or authorize access. The access token is sent as usual, for example with the `Bearer` scheme ({{BEARER}}), and the proof contains an `ath` claim as specified in {{Section 4.2 of DPOP}}.
```

reviews.author: PieterKas
reviews.body:
Thanks for this. Binding the access token to a key the protected resource vouches for is a useful addition, and it lets a protected resource step up from a bearer token to a sender-constrained token for a specific transaction. Requesting changes for the following:

Terminology. “Key-bound challenge” suggests the challenge itself is bound to a key or carries a proof. It isn’t: it carries a key that the access token should be bound to. I’ve suggested renaming the section to “Access Token Key Binding” (#access-token-key-binding) and using “binding key” or “challenge that contains a cnf claim” throughout. Note that the heading at line 457 also needs renaming, or the updated cross-references will break.

Alignment with RFC 9449. Sending a DPoP proof with a bearer token, or with no access token at all, goes beyond what RFC 9449 defines. The text should say explicitly that this extends RFC 9449. Please also either define the token-less case fully or remove it.

Signalling. The 401 a client receives when it should add a DPoP proof to a bearer request looks the same as an RFC 9449 request for a DPoP-bound token, so a standard client will go and get a DPoP-bound token instead. Please define an explicit signal, such as an error parameter or protected resource metadata, and add an example.

Authorization server trust model. The authorization server binds the token to a key whose possession it never verifies; it relies on the protected resource’s signed assertion. Please state this explicitly, and note that it overrides the client’s DPoP policy.

Readability. I’ve suggested shorter rewrites of the Security Considerations paragraphs.

comments.body:
Yes, your read is correct and both are intended. I was pushing the existing signaling too far.

We should distinguish “retry with the bearer token plus a proof” from “present a DPoP-bound token.” A transaction-specific parameter seems reasonable, while preserving the existing meaning of `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP`.

For example, we could add `key_proof="dpop"` to the `Bearer` transaction-authorization error:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="transaction_authorization_required", key_proof="dpop", algs="ES256"
```

The requester would retry with the existing bearer token and a fresh DPoP proof, including `ath` for that token. The RS would omit `transaction_challenge` until it validates the proof. We would define `algs` here as the acceptable proof-signing algorithms and retain `Bearer` plus `key_proof="dpop"` on proof and nonce errors.

@bc-pi Do you see any issues with using the DPoP proof format this way?
